title: Simple QKD keyrate computations from tangent-line bounds
authors: Jun Hui Goh, Ernest Y. -Z. Tan
abstract: Recent work in quantum key distribution (QKD) has yielded finite-size keyrates based on convex optimisation problems, using the framework of entropy accumulation. Multiple solvers have been developed to address these optimisations in recent years, but have been based on a somewhat elaborate framework using sophisticated algorithms, in order to accommodate a broad range of QKD protocols. In this work, we note that for basic QKD protocols such as qubit BB84, the keyrates can be easily computed using off-the-shelf solvers instead, by obtaining suitable tangent lines to lower bound terms in the objective function. We compute the resulting finite-size keyrates and compare them to previous work. Moreover, we extend this approach to the six-state protocol, by deriving closed-form expressions for the single-round Rényi entropies in the protocol. This should facilitate subsequent study of the six-state protocol via entropy accumulation.
summary: This paper develops a novel, computationally efficient method to calculate certified lower bounds on the keyrates for QKD protocols like BB84. By reformulating complex optimization problems using tangent-line approximations, the authors make these calculations tractable for standard convex solvers. This advances the theoretical understanding of achievable secure key rates in quantum cryptography.
main_problem: The paper addresses the computation of finite-size keyrates for Quantum Key Distribution (QKD) protocols, aiming to provide certified lower bounds.
main_result: The authors propose using tangent-line approximations to transform complex, non-convex optimization problems into computationally tractable convex forms, yielding certified lower bounds for the keyrate.
method: The core method involves reformulating the keyrate optimization problem to utilize convex optimization solvers by deriving suitable tangent lines to the lower bound terms in the objective function.
model_or_system: The analysis focuses on QKD protocols, specifically the qubit BB84 and the six-state protocol, often modeled using entanglement-based forms and Werner states.
key_observables: Finite-size keyrate ($\ell_{	ext{key}}$), Rényi entropy ($	ext{H}^{\uparrow}_{\alpha}, 	ext{H}^{\downarrow}_{\alpha}$), and the asymptotic keyrate ($	ext{r}_{	ext{asymp}}$).
important_parameters: Rényi entropy parameter ($\alpha$), security parameter ($\varepsilon_{	ext{secure}}$), and test-round probability ($\gamma$).
main_assumptions: The keyrate bound is derived using a tangent-line lower bound approximation, meaning the computed rate is guaranteed to be less than or equal to the true achievable rate.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the convergence of the computed keyrate as the number of tangent lines or the grid size increases, showing the rate plateaus at sufficient computational effort.
paper_structure: The paper first introduces the general problem of keyrate computation via convex optimization, then details the tangent-line approximation technique for simple protocols like BB84, and finally extends this to derive closed-form entropy expressions for the six-state protocol.
why_interesting: The rigorous mathematical techniques developed for bounding keyrates using convex optimization and tangent lines provide powerful, generalizable tools for analyzing information-theoretic security in quantum communication.

The plot is not monotone because for each ntangent we took the tangent lines at uniformly spaced points over Q ∈[0, 1], which results in the set of tangent lines for each ntangent not being a subset of those for ntangent + 1.
FIG. 2. Plot of keyrate value as the grid size of the grid search increases. 100 tangent lines were used in the approximation of the convex optimisation.

The purple graph plots the values com- puted by the original authors. The blue graph plots the val- ues computed using the proposed methodology, with the val- ues of α and γ found in [1]. The dashed black line shows the asymptotic keyrate for our parameter choices, which is rasymp = 0.663.
